subtopic: HOCKEY-WINNING OF ALLAN CUP BY EDMONTON FLYERS
HOCKEY-WINNING OF ALLAN CUP BY EDMONTON FLYERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. I know, sir, that at times you have granted the privilege to some other members on matters similar to that which I wish to bring up, and I am sure that hon. members will bear with me, especially in view of the fact that it is noncontentious.
Tlie matter I wish to bring to the attention of the house, and of the people as well, carries a lesson which I hope we shall all take to heart. Last Saturday, sir, in the city of Calgary, in the province of Alberta, the Edmonton Flyers, representing the great city of Edmonton, won the senior championship in hockey, our national game, with the result that the Allan cup now rests in Edmonton. The lesson I wish to convey is this. Forty years ago, which is a long time in anyone's life, the young and ambitious city of Edmonton challenged for the Stanley cup and went to Montreal to play the Wanderers-and, by the way, they lost only by a goal or two.
The president of the Edmonton club in that year was none other than the genial member for Edmonton West (Mr. MacKinnon), who is still with us and has been a member of the cabinet for many years.
Only one more minute of your time do I wish to take up, Mr. Speaker. When we hear so much about things being "fixed," when there is so much suspicion cast around, I think it is well for our young people to learn the lesson of this game in Calgary on Saturday night. Two great teams faced each other when the series stood at three for Edmonton Flyers and one for Ottawa Senators. If Ottawa had won that game it would have meant that the teams would leave for Edmonton, where the largest gate in the history of Edmonton in a hockey game would have been assured, carrying a revenue of some $25,000. I heard the opinion expressed on the street that the Flyers would lose so that they would go back to Edmonton to play. Sir, they did not lose. They won the game in the last few minutes, putting everything they had into it. The club and the
players lost $25,000, but they proved to the people of Canada that integrity, honesty and honour still exist in this country, and that they cannot be bought.

speechtext:
I desire to move:
That the advisability of continuing the publication of the revised edition of debates and distribution of the unrevised edition of same be referred to the standing committee on debates.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ADVISABILITY OF CONTINUING PUBLICATION OF REVISED EDITION-MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is the Secretary of State not going to explain what is involved in this motion?

subtopic: ADVISABILITY OF CONTINUING PUBLICATION OF REVISED EDITION-MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It has
been brought to my attention that the practice of printing the revised edition of debates is an expensive operation both in time and in money. For the last year for which we have the complete figures-that is the edition of 1944-it required over 4,000 hours of work on the linotype machines, nearly 9,000 hours of hand work, and over 1,500 hours of press work, all of which could have been utilized to better advantage and at the same time provide a saving of time and space. On account of Hansard having to be reprinted for the revised edition, it is necessary each session to keep standing about 16,000 pages of type, involving some 88 tons of metal. That occupies a large section of the printing bureau's space which is required for other purposes. The printing of the revised edition of Hansard of 1944, which comprised 510 sets of volumes in English and in French, cost approximately $75 a set. With the increase in wages and in printing costs since 1944, it is estimated that the total cost will run to something about $46,000. I understand that revised editions of debates are not produced in Washington, London or France. It is proposed that the committee give consideration to doing away with the revised edition here, thereby making a considerable saving of expense.

subtopic: ADVISABILITY OF CONTINUING PUBLICATION OF REVISED EDITION-MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask a question of the Secretary of State? Do I understand that a bound edition will be published, on better paper than that on which Hansard is printed? The daily Hansard will be bound and will be available as a permanent record of parliament; is that the idea?

speechtext: That will be considered by the committee. I understand that if the daily edition is to be bound, it will be available to members within two or three months after the house prorogues, rather than about a year later as is the case with the revised edition at the present time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ADVISABILITY OF CONTINUING PUBLICATION OF REVISED EDITION-MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE

May I make a suggestion to the Secretary of State? First of all I think there is merit in the proposal to refer to the standing committee on debates the matters covered by this motion. I would point out, however, that it is a number of years since the debates committee last met, and it is possible that there are a number of other matters which the committee might like to discuss.

Private Bills
When committees meet we find sometimes that we are prevented, by the limitations imposed by the terms of reference, from considering matters in which members may be interested. Actually this motion is rather broad, but I should like to ask the Secretary of State if he would consider having added after the word "same" in the last line some such words as "and any other matters relating to the debates". The purpose would be to give freedom to the committee, under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), to discuss other matters without the bother of having to come back to the house. The Secretary of State may feel that the terms of reference are wide enough. If he would give the assurance that so far as he is concerned other matters could be discussed, that would be satisfactory. When we get into committee we are governed by the rules, but I am sure it would help if we had some understanding that, when the committee meets, there will be fairly wide latitude for the discussion of matters relating to debates, which after all is the purpose of the committee.

speechtext:
1.	Negotiations have been completed for the sale of a number of wartime housing units in North Vancouver.

4.	Terms: (a) A purchaser may buy for all cash. If he wishes immediate title he will be required to pay the full sale price; if he agrees to reside in the house for five years and obtain title at the end of that period, provided he does not default under the terms of the agreement, he will be allowed a discount of 174 per cent on the sale price. The reduced amount that he will be required to pay is known as the anticipated price.
(b) A purchaser may buy on deferred payment plan with a minimum down payment of 10 per cent and six months' taxes in advance. The balance is payable in monthly instalments which approximate his current rental over a period not exceeding twenty-five years. The standard contract provides for a reduction from the sale price to the anticipated price if the purchaser or his immediate family occupy the house for five years from the date of purchase and comply with the terms of their agreement. The monthly payments cover principal and interest, insurance and one-twelfth of the yearly taxes. The corporation undertakes to install permanent foundation walls, replace metal chimneys with masonry ones and where two adjoining properties are served by a double woodshed, to divide the same and move each half into its appropriate lot.
Prices: Average anticipated prices are: Small 4-room, $2,500; large 4-room, $2,750; 6-room, $3,200.

6.	Tenants who do not wish to purchase may be asked to move to suitable alternative accommodation. If a tenant is moved to a smaller house than he now occupies, it must be suitable to house his family without overcrowding. A tenant will not be required to move more than once and a veteran will not be moved to accommodate a non-veteran. Furthermore, tenants who are required to move will be compensated for moving expenses by a grant up to but not in excess of $15.

speechtext:
1.	Can the Ministry of National Health and Welfare say whether or not the committee of inquiry set up in New South Wales, Australia, to investigate the Braund treatment for cancer nas completed its inquiries?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-BRAUND TREATMENT FOR CANCER
speechtext:
1.	Yes. The committee has completed its inquiries and its report was tabled in the New South Wales parliament on April 8.
2.	The report states that the committee found Braund's treatment was in no way a specific cure for cancer, nor could it retard the growth of cancer. The committee concluded from patients examined that Braund in no case had substantiated his claim to cure cancer.
On March 9, in reply to a question by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), I informed the house that the Department of National Health and Welfare had directed inquiries to the government of New South Wales regarding the alleged Braund cure for cancer. At that time I reported the receipt of a preliminary report from the chairman of the committee appointed to investigate Mr. Braund's treatment, which recommended strongly against patients going to Australia for the purpose of receiving that treatment. I am now able to inform the house that the investigating committee's report was tabled in the New South Wales parliament on April 8. The report states that the committee found Braund's treatment was in no way a specific cure for cancer, nor could it retard the growth of cancer. They concluded from patients examined that Braund in no case had substantiated his claim to cure cancer.

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): The hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Haekett) raised a question on May 4, 1948, concerning the appearance before the Ontario municipal board of the consul general of the United States in Toronto. At that time I gave an undertaking that I would inquire into this incident and report to the house.
By international custom or treaty, and in accordance with instructions from their home states, consuls perform functions pertaining to the promotion of commerce and industry, the supervision of merchant shipping, protection for nationals of the appointing state, and certain notarial functions.
In the performance of these functions pertaining to commerce and industry, consuls must be allowed by the receiving state to watch over the execution of commercial treaties, to send reports to the home state on everything which can influence the development of its commerce and industry, and to give information to merchants and manufacturers of the appointing state necessary for the protection of their commercial interests. It is also generally admitted that in addition to the exercise of these duties of protection, consuls
may render certain assistance and help to their nationals who may be litigants before the courts of the jurisdiction where they perform their functions.
It seems clear in international law that a diplomatic envoy cannot be compelled or even requested to appear in a court as a witness in a civil, criminal or administrative procedure. But if he chooses to appear the courts may, and usually do, allow him to do so. By analogy, though there does not appear to be any clear rule of international law on this point, it would seem that a consul may ask a court within his consular jurisdiction to hear his statement on any matter in which the local interests of a national of his state may be involved. The court, of course, having control of its procedure, may decide the conditions upon which a statement may be given, and, having heard it, decide what weight, if any, should be attached to it.
In this particular instance, public notice had been given by the Ontario municipal board that it would hear the application of the M. & G. Convoy Company of Buffalo for a licence to carry automobiles in bond over provincial highways from one point in the United States to another. I understand it is the practice of the board to hear anyone whose statement is expected to be relevant. In the case of Mr. Russell, the chairman of the board decided to allow him to be heard. It is also our information that the proceedings of the board are usually informal and that witnesses are rarely put under oath.
I am informed that the consul general was acting in conformity with instructions from the United States Department of State, and for this reason he felt that he could not properly take an oath or be examined as an ordinary witness. This is quite clear from the letter he sent to the chairman of the Ontario municipal board on April 30. If I understood his statement aright the hon. member for Stanstead said it was competent to the board to receive a letter which would not be received as proof in an ordinary court of justice. I should like to read the letter sent to the chairman of the Ontario municipal board on April 30; I think it puts the matter in its proper perspective:
American Consulate General, Toronto 1, Canada, April 30, 1948
The Honourable
Chairman, Ontario Municipal Board, Parliament Buildings,
Toronto.
Sir:
I have the honour to refer to the hearing before your board on the morning of April 29, 1948, and beg to confirm herewith my verbal statement at that time . . .
Inquiries oj the Ministry

The United States government is very much interested in the general proposal of freedom of movement by American trucking interests carrying in transit goods across Ontario from Michigan to New York, including this present application of M & G Convoy, Incorporated.
The consulate general in Toronto hopes for a favourable decision at an early date in this case by your honourable board. There may be other similar applications.
As my statement was made officially, I could not properly take oath to it or be examined or cross-examined upon it.
Respectfully yours,
H. Earle Russell, American Consul General.
It seems that all this amounted to, in fact, was to express before the Ontario municipal board what was well known to be the attitude of the United States with respect to this matter. This gentleman, in the exercise of his official functions, was seeking to render assistance to and further the commercial interests of nationals of his country before an administrative board. Whatever view may be taken of such an official act we must not forget that Canada too sends consuls abroad. When His Majesty issues a commission to the Canadian consul His Majesty grants-and I quote the language of the commission-
. . . full power and authority by all lawful means to aid and protect those Canadian citizens who may trade with or visit or reside within his consular district.
I therefore think this incident should not be magnified into one of considerable significance. In view of the controversial nature of this question and the discussions which have been going on about it for some time, however, I regret that it was considered necessary or advisable for the United States consul general in Toronto to ask to be heard by the provincial municipal board at this time.

subtopic: ARRANGEMENT FOR SHIPMENT OF CANADIAN- OWNED COMBINES TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the arrangement
for the shipment of Canadian-owned combines to the United States is made by officials of the Department of Labour in Ottawa with the Department of Labour at Washington. Then the Department of Labour in Washington secures clearance through the United States immigration and customs officials. This has been going on for a number of years, as my hon. friend knows. It was developed more particularly during the war years. Last year 1,100 combines went to various parts of the central and southern states; this was the biggest movement on record. The average in previous years was about 600.
Might I add in passing that millions of dollars have been earned by this movement. Last year 412 of the owners of combines reported that they had received $3,325,000, which indicates that the owners of the 1,100 machines received close to $8,000,000, all in United States funds.
The movement from the United States to Canada is not as great. At most there have been 40 American combines taking part in this movement. I am informed that this year it is not expected that as many Canadian combines will be required by the United States, because of the late crop, particularly in New Mexico, Oklahoma and Texas.
I might mention also the very friendly relations we have in connection with the movement of workers from Restigouche county in New Brunswick to Maine for the potato harvest, and from the southern part of Quebec for the lumber operations also in Maine. Then there is the movement of tobacco workers from the southern states into Ontario for the harvesting of the crop there.
When the movement does take place the selection will be made, as in the past, by the farm labour directors of the respective provinces; and of the dominion, which are involved in the movement.

speechtext:
On Thursday last I asked whether it would be possible for Canada to embark on a program of prefabricated houses. The Toronto Daily Star gave wide coverage to my remarks, for which I am grateful to the reporter who represents that paper here in Ottawa. The result was that on Friday, Saturday and Sunday I was swamped with telephone calls, and I have received a great many letters here asking about the prefabrication program. There are quite a number of housing schemes around Toronto. I have seen some of them, and the prices are away beyond anything that I would pay. In all the groups that I have seen I would not pay more than S3,000 for any house.
People are anxious to get houses at reasonable prices. As I said on Thursday, under no circumstances can a working man afford to
pay S6.000 or $8,000 for a house, nor can he afford to pay a rental running as high as $80. Would it be possible for Canada to do what they ane doing in England and France with prefabricated houses?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Canada is using prefabricated houses in some sections. I think there are five substantial producers of prefabricated houses. The difficulty is the buyer's resistance; there is no fully prefabricated house that has entirely broken down the resistance of buyers. All houses built by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are prefabricated to some extent. Panels are built off the job, and other work is done off site.
Another difficulty in connection with fully prefabricated houses is the meeting of local building bylaws. My hon. friend will recall that the Fairchild aircraft company produced prefabricated houses back in 1945 and 1946. These were substantial houses, and they met most of the requirements for a small house. But the difficulty was to meet the various building bylaws. Resistance developed to such an extent that the Fairchild house went off the market.
There is a preference among house buyers for the style with which they are familiar. I happened to be in southern California two or three years ago when an aircraft company there was considering going into prefabricated housing. Before doing so they decided to hold a competition to determine what design of house would be most acceptable to the buyer. They built one standard Cape Cod cottage, a style of small house which we all know in Canada, and two prefabricated houses. They took a ballot as to which was most acceptable to the public and 85 per cent of those voting favoured the standard Cape Cod cottages as against the two prefabricated designs. It is a combination of these circumstances which holds down the number of prefabricated houses that are being brought into use. One contractor in London, Ontario, who builds prefabricated houses, and moves them to a site in the neighbourhood, is working to capacity, but the plant has a very small capacity. He has a house which is acceptable in the London area and meets the bylaws of the city. About the only way I can see to bring about a much larger use of prefabricated houses would be to have localized operations of that kind, to meet the conditions of the particular locality.
