speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, April 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. MacKinnon for the second reading of Bill No. 209, to amend the National Parks Act.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF PARK DESCRIPTIONS-REGULATIONS EFFECTIVE WHEN PUBLISHED IN "CANADA GAZETTE"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 28 I had spoken briefly on this bill, and had referred particularly to the national park in New Brunswick. At that time I had stated that the people of that province were greatly pleased that a national park was to be established there. However, they had felt that the establishment of a park had been delayed much longer than was necessary.
 .
I had also pointed out that some surprise had been expressed as to the site of the national park, in view of the fact that inspectors of the federal government who inspected different sites in the province had selected another one. I would take this opportunity to read the report presented by Mr. J. Smart, chief inspector of national parks. In this report he referred to the examination of a proposed national park in New Brunswick. At page 4 of the report referring to the Mount Champlain site on the St. John river, the one which I understand was his choice, he said:
In Mr. Cautley's report of his 1936 examination of park sites for New Brunswick, he has covered very fully the features of Mount Champ-plain and I agree with him that this site is the most suitable for a park establishment, when considering it with the Lepreau and Albert county sites. It is true that the Mount Champlain site is not on the sea coast but this is rather a benefit on account of the drawbacks to the bay of Fundy coast, which is subject to frequent cold fogs, high tides, and the water is for the most part always in a riled condition due to the ebb and flow of the tide, and always very cold.
Those are not my views. I do not agree entirely with the views expressed here by Mr. Smart and Mr. Cautley with respect to the situation along the bay of Fundy. Then the report goes on:
Further, in making a comparison with the Lepreau and Albert county sites, consideration is given to the fact that the provincial government in acquiring it will not have such a heavy financial obligation as would be the case for the other sites. On the other hand the federal government will not have an expensive site to develop.
I shall not read the full report, but it sums up to the opinion expressed by these different men to the effect that the site on the St. John river, known as the Mount Champlain site, is, by considerable odds, the best in New Brunswick.
Mr. Smart closes his report in this way:
Some additional features which commend this site as a national park site, particularly in regard to developments:
1.	Number 2 provincial trunk highway passes through the portion on the river frontage. This highway is now paved to within about five miles of the proposed southerly boundary on the river frontage.
2.	Hydro electric power distribution passes through the area.
3.	The Canadian National Railways pass through the river frontage with a station located on the site.
4.	The Canadian Pacific railway main line has a station at Westfield within three miles on the park boundary and on the main highway.
5.	Passenger boat service available from all points between Fredericton and Saint John.
6.	Mount Champlain site is not too close to United States boundary.

National Parks Act
7.	Central to the larger centres of population of New Brunswick.
8.	Development costs will be low as compared with the establishment of other parks in Canada.
9.	Future administration costs will he low. A minimum personnel will be required to administer it.
10.	Ease of game and fire protection.
My point is that, in view of the report made by the inspectors from Ottawa, I would ask the minister why this site on the St. John river was passed over in favour of another site in New Brunswick. When I ask that question I should like to have it understood that, since it means nothing to me personally, I have no objection to the choice of any site in particular. However, when money has been spent to send inspectors to New Brunswick-and they went there on numerous occasions

I believe the people of that province should know why this site was chosen.
While I am on my feet, I should like to speak about national parks in general. There can be no question that they are one of the greatest assets we have in Canada. They offer the greatest attraction for tourist trade from all sections of Canada, and draw many thousands, perhaps millions, of citizens from the United States, who spend large sums in this country.
One point, however, which has occurred to me is that while we advertise to encourage United States tourists to come to this country, I believe we should try to have the people from one part of Canada visit other sections. Perhaps this could be done through our parks branch better than in any other way. During the war one would hear young men from different parts of Canada say, when in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick where they happened to be stationed in camps, "Had it not been for the war, we would never have seen this part of Canada." I believe that is true.
In my province I have seen thousands of cars every year from every state in the United States, but it is seldom that we see a oar from British Columbia or Manitoba or Saskatchewan. The result is that we in this country are strangers to one another. Means should be devised, through our national parks and through an interprovincial highway, whereby our people could visit the different sections of Canada. That would be all to the good as far as the unity of this great country is concerned. I recommend to the dominion government the construction of the trans-Canada and any other highways that are needed in order to bring our people closer together.
We have a good precedent from the days of confederation when one of the great bonds to join the different parts of the cquntry together was the railroad from the Atlantic to the Pacific. A great interprovincial highway would go far to join the different parts of Canada together.
It is not my intention to say anything more, but I do want to ask why this site in New Brunswick was chosen, because I am sure the people in that province will want to know.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF PARK DESCRIPTIONS-REGULATIONS EFFECTIVE WHEN PUBLISHED IN "CANADA GAZETTE"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not think we would reach this bill as quickly as we have done, but I wish to say a word or two about the national parks' about which I know something, namely the three parks in Alberta. I hope that what I say will not be regarded as critical of any individual. Other provinces can speak for themselves, but I want to say that in those parks in which there are mountainous areas we have the most neglected of all the natural resources owned by the dominion government. It may be true to say it is easy to criticize, but this is one place where I hope criticisms will be helpful.
We have Banff, Jasper and Waterford parks. Some money has been spent, but it has been very little. I should like to deal first with the winter aspect. Competent persons who have skied in Switzerland and Austria inform me that we have snow conditions and ski runs in those areas which cannot be equalled anywhere in Europe. There is, however, a complete lack of accommodation for people who would go there. We have all heard of Sun Valley, I think, in Idaho in the United States, but we also know they have seasons when there is no snow at all. Therefore it has become a rather hit-or-miss place of amusement and entertainment.
In the three parks in the western part of our province we have conditions for winter sports not met with anywhere else, with the possible exception of the large mountain just outside Seattle, the name of which I have forgotten.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF PARK DESCRIPTIONS-REGULATIONS EFFECTIVE WHEN PUBLISHED IN "CANADA GAZETTE"
speechtext: It is Mount Baker on the right.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF PARK DESCRIPTIONS-REGULATIONS EFFECTIVE WHEN PUBLISHED IN "CANADA GAZETTE"
speechtext:
The hon. member tells me that it is Mount Baker. There is nowhere else in the world where they have that sort of thing. I am not saying anything against skiing in the Laurentians. I have visited two or three of the more famous places and I have no doubt that skiing conditions are excellent. One thing I did notice was how important this sport is in Montreal
National Parks Act

and Ottawa. On week ends literally trainloads of people go out to these places.
I happen to be a life member of a ski club in Banff. We have tried, without receiving very much assistance, to do something to provide accommodation for skiers. They finally have what I believe is called a tow, so that it does not mean that you go downhill in a hurry and then take all afternoon to get back again for a second shot at it.
In the summer time we put a few fish in the streams. At Banff there is a small hatchery which is doing a good job. It is unfortunate that when they chlorinated the water there they did not advise the hatchery, because scores of thousands of fish which were coming along nicely died as a result. There was no liaison between the fisheries and the public works which had to do with the chlorination of the water.
In the province there is a brewing company which is operating, at its own expense, a splendid hatchery in Calgary. It is one of the places that we suggest strangers should visit. They have fish there in all sizes. Then there is the question of housing in the town of Banff which is in a most unsatisfactory condition. They have been talking for years about beautifying Banff, but progress is at least slow.
What I have in mind is this. We need a complete revamping of the administration of our national parks. It is unfortunate that ministers do not seem to stay long in this portfolio, and it is still more unfortunate that the hon. gentleman who has had that portfolio since I came here has been ill for the last year or so. I should like nothing better than that the acting minister should have the portfolio because, as we learned today, it took him forty years to make a winning hockey club in Edmonton. He must have had tremendous vision to look forty years ahead. I played against the fellows they had there when he was president, and they were not nearly as good as the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene) tells us.
We need someone at the head of the department who will do more than the patchwork which is now being done with our parks. There is no other place in the world better suited for the holding of the winter Olympic games than Banff in the national park of that name. People are always afraid of what it will cost, but money laid out in the next few years will bring greater returns to this country than anything else I know of. The tourist dollar is just as good as the dollar of anyone else.

It so happens that I know something of these mountains. I have had at least twenty or thirty pack trips centering on Banff and lake Louise, and going into and through those mountains, and anyone who thinks he can see the mountains from a train or a motorcar simply does not know what he is missing. In other words, you must do it on foot, or on the back of a mountain horse, and the horses walk all the time on these pack trips, so they will not trip you down the side of a gully or anything like that. The beauty which is there and the resources, resources in the sense that you can get a dollar from people for looking at something- why, the eastern slope of those mountains is a treasure house that nobody really knows anything about. At the present time, if one does go to see them he is so worried and burdened with the idea of trying to find a place to sleep and eat or something of that kind that the place has fallen into disrepute.
What I am asking from this government is this, that when the minister who is now acting decides that he is no longer going to act but to take his ease which he has well earned, not in the other place but in some other place-I am not appointing him over there because he is too valuable here-

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF PARK DESCRIPTIONS-REGULATIONS EFFECTIVE WHEN PUBLISHED IN "CANADA GAZETTE"
speechtext: He would not refuse the other place.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF PARK DESCRIPTIONS-REGULATIONS EFFECTIVE WHEN PUBLISHED IN "CANADA GAZETTE"
speechtext:
That is something, with great respect, which the hon. member does not know, although if the minister accepts my advice he will go there.
What we need and need so badly is a complete reorganization of the department. Remember, I am not complaining about the individuals in it, not for one minute. But for a tremendous problem like this you must have leadership. You cannot have the department head perhaps cutting off his own head by leading the pack too far. What we need in those parks is some place where the average fellow can take his jalopy and go up there and find a meal that will not break him, and find a bed to sleep in, camp grounds, and all that kind of thing.
There is no reason why our golf courses, for example, in the two parks, the one at Banff and the one at Jasper, should be so expensive. A man must be almost a millionaire in order to have a round of golf on those very fine courses. Much of the dominion's money went into those courses. It is perfectly true that now the one in Jasper is operated by the Canadian National Railways and the one in Banff has been turned back and is operated by the Canadian Pacific Railway

National Parks Act
Company, but the people of Canada largely paid for those courses.
I had occasion to speak to the acting minister the other day and I must say that he gave me his confidence and his complete concurrence in the idea which the younger men in the Gyro club at Banff have. They told me, and I conveyed this to the minister, that what they want is a sports director, somebody who would bell the people where to go and what they would find when they got there. They are not asking for any money from the dominion government to pay this man. A man of this type should never be a civil servant. Their idea is to have owners of hotels and rooming houses, cottages, these bungalow camps, and so on, charge the small matter of ten cents added to the night's lodging, and the Gyro club would administer that and employ someone who knew the business of sports director. This is done in many skiing places in the United States. In that way a fund would be got together which would not cost the government anything. All that the club is seeking is the permission of the government to make arrangements with these people to charge the extra ten cents and turn it over to them, to be expended by them; but in order to do that they require the consent of the government, because the government is in charge of the rates for sleeping and eating accommodation.
Let me again repeat that the acting minister received me with the greatest of sympathy and co-operation and I trust that shortly that small thing will have been accomplished. But I only look at that as a beginning of the great things which may be done. These are modem days of good roads, and even in that far-off part of the country we have now good roads to both places. I think the Edmonton-Jasper road has been completed and affords an enjoyable drive.
Here we have a bill setting out these areas, territories and so on. What we need is not a gentle prodding of those responsible for the national parks in this country, but we need to give them encouragement. The present men are all right, but we need to give them a few dollars to spend, and let us have in the operation a little less of centralized government. When you think, Mr. Speaker, that you can scarcely do anything, certainly nothing of any account, in a national park without reference to Ottawa, you will immediately see how difficult it is to make any progress. That is not the fault of the officials, nor am I going to blame the government for it. It is our fault in this House of Commons because we have not interested ourselves enough in one of our greatest assets, to convert it into what it
should be; first, a great national playground for our own people, and, then, a money-making institution, the money to be derived from those persons who would visit us here in the Dominion of Canada.
I close with one sentence, since I see it is just about six o'clock. It is a repetition, if you like; but it is this, that we here try to realize what an asset these places are. Look abroad and see what they have done in other countries without anything like the natural facilities that we have. Then we shall come to appreciate ourselves and provide these conveniences, and the return of good will and in money will be beyond belief in this Dominion of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon we had a couple of interesting and appreciative talks about our national parks, but the hon. gentlemen who were speaking about them confined themselves to New Brunswick, the maritime provinces and British Columbia. I thought what they said about the beauties of their respective parts of the country was well said, because we do possess a wonderful heritage of beauty and grandeur in Canada.
I had the privilege two years ago of motoring around the Cabot trail, driving through the Annapolis valley, visiting Annapolis Royal and seeing what was done there to reconstruct the first French fortress in North America, and I can also emphasize what the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) said this afternoon with regard to the Rocky mountains.
I should like, however, to point out that quite often the prairie land is thought of as rather flat and uninteresting country whereas it is nothing of the kind. Across the prairie land there are beautiful valleys and lakes, and not only has the national parks branch taken advantage of some of these beauty spots, but, I am glad to say, the provinces have done so also. I am thinking of my own province of Saskatchewan and a lovely little resort around Carlyle lake district where, during the depression, the government of the day built a chalet to give accommodation to people from the United States as well as from Canada.
In the northern part of Saskatchewan we have the Prince Albert national park at Waskesiu. There is a playground in that whole northern region, not only for the prairie province of Saskatchewan but for the people

That can certainly not be said to have been done by any generation of Canadians that has yet lived.
I have often thought we give too little attention to our wild animals throughout the country. When we travel over the area from Winnipeg to Port Arthur and on to Sudbury, going through reaches that look to be worthless when judged according to ordinary standards, we are actually passing over regions of Canada that I have thought could be made into extensive and attractive parks which would draw tourists from all over the world.
We should be taking much more care than we are taking of our game birds, fish and parks.
Since the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) has mentioned our parks, I think it only fitting that I should say a word or two in appreciation of the parks of Alberta.
The park in my constituency is the Water-ton Lakes park. If any hon. members happen to be out in southwestern Canada, they will miss a rare treat if they fail to visit Waterton Lakes park. The people around that country all call it "Wonderful Waterton", and wonderful Waterton it is, with its vast and varied mountains; its lakes of great number, size and beauty; and its streams with more than one romantic waterfall. All these things tend to make it a place of great attractiveness. There are forests in the park. It is true they are not comparable with some of those found in certain other areas of Canada, but for that particular region they are respectable forests. There are wilderness trails in Waterton Lakes park. One can drive along on the Akimina highway, for example, and three minutes after leaving Waterton Lake townsite, can feel himself completely lost and alone; and unless he had a guide or a good road to get him back, he would be lost. But there is a good road to get him back.
There are numerous wild animals. There are not many places in Canada where you can drive along the road and have a bear cross your path and dodge into the thicket, or a deer or elk-run along a little way in front of you and dash off into a ravine. But you can have these pleasing experiences on the Akimina highway of Waterton Lakes park.
At one time this park used to be famous for its fish. Men used to travel by wagon for a hundred miles in order to be able to fish in the great lakes which are the main attraction in Waterton Lakes park, and which have given it its name. I regret to tell the minister that these fish are no longer abundant. It is no longer easy to catch them. In fact people are often greatly disappointed when they come to Waterton Lakes park, having heard of its fame as a fishing centre, and find themselves unable to catch any fish.
The park is unique in Canada because it adjoins Glacier national park which is on the other side of the United States border. The two parks together have been formed into an international peace park. In the Glacier national park there is the Logan highway which is, I think, one of the greatest attractions to be found in western north America.
AH these things go to show that the Water-ton Lakes national park is a potential treasure house for Canada with regard to tourists. We should be able to make it, to United States tourists, one of the greatest attractions for thousands of miles.
There are two or three things about this park to which the minister would be well advised to give attention. One of these is the fish. People will travel a long way in order to fish. We in Canada should be able to go and have a pleasing holiday fishing whenever we
National Parks Act

choose. There is a fish hatchery at Waterton Lakes park, but it is not in any way capable of discharging the responsibilities which ought to be attached to a fish hatchery. I fancy that it can supply, year after year, just about one-tenth as many fish as it needs to be able to supply. There are a number of problems associated with improving the efficiency of that fish hatchery. I do not wish to disparage the men who are in charge of the fish hatchery; I think they have done the best they could with the means at their disposal. But that whole matter of the fish hatchery should be given genuine attention, with the determination to make the fish hatchery discharge the function it ought to discharge with respect to that park.
The suggestion has been made-and I throw it out to the minister as worth considering- that supplementary breeding pools for the fish could be established at various points along certain small creeks in the neighbourhood; for example, Fish creek, that runs through the village of Mountain View. Along Fish creek a good many ponds could be made in which small fish could be raised from the time they were taken from the hatchery until they could be safely put into the open waters where they would have to look after themselves. This little creek could be used because, being a small stream running along through the valleys, its waters are warmer than those of the lakes immediately adjoining the fish hatchery, and warm water is much more conducive to the growth of the vegetable matter which the fish eat in their younger stages. In some parts of the United States they tell me they put into the water a special kind of fertilizer which encourages the growth of the plant life used by the fish.
It is suggested that if this stream is made into pools, as it could be, together with two or three other creeks such as Lee creek, which runs down from the mountains into Cardston, we could increase the productiveness and effectiveness of that fish hatchery at least tenfold. This ought to be done. Then the fish could remain in the pools until they could be moved into the open waters, and during that period they would be free from the danger of the larger fish. I suggest that the minister give this very careful attention and have the members of his department go to work on the problem, not next year but right away. If they say there are difficulties in the way, let the minister say, "Very well; we want you to remove those difficulties. That is exactly what you are on the job to do. We want results, and no excuses."
I am positive, if the minister says this to his officials and gives them the money with

which to accomplish results, they will do so, and it will pay us many times over in United States dollars.
There is another difficulty in the park. In times past the people established a townsite there of which they ane very proud. They have become a bit choosey, if I may use that word, with respect to the houses. They do not want cabins that are not equal in size, appearance, romantic appeal, and all the rest of it, to those built by the more or less wealthy people who first went into the area and built themselves summer cottages. Nevertheless we must have, in connection with Waterton Lakes park, a great many cabins which will not be too costly to the tourists. We must have enough cabins so tourists will not be warned away and perhaps go to some other place for the night, making Waterton Lakes park merely a place to visit in the daytime. There must be tourist cabins. I would not like to suggest to the minister just how many cabins should be erected, or how costly they should be, or just w'here they should be located, but again I say he should tell the members of his department that he wants enough tourist cabins put up in and around the park to accommodate all the tourists who may come to Waterton lakes in a year. All the cabins might be left in charge of one of the businessmen there, with instructions to render them available when they were called for.
I am not sure that we can depend upon private enterprise for these cabins. I would be inclined to think the government should own the tourist cabins, because it wants to have spent in Canada all the United States dollars that can be brought here.

Men who have played on the finest courses in America tell me they know of no other course anywhere on this continent that surpasses this golf course. The great criticism of the national parks in British Columbia is, first of all, that they are too far away from the people of that province. Most of the really good parks are on the Alberta side of the Rocky mountains, in Banff and in Jasper. Until recently the cost of staying in one of those places was beyond the resources of the average Canadian on holiday. I think it is a truism to say that there are far more people in New York who visit our national parks in the Rockies than there are in Vancouver.
The location of the parks is one thing, and the type of accommodation which is afforded is another. The Rocky mountain parks are six hundred miles by road from Vancouver, and the roads are poor. I do not like to use the people of the United States as an example, but in the state of Washington to the south of us the people have shown what can be done in developing territory such as we have for the use of the people. At Mount Baker, some few miles from the city of Bellingham; at Mount Rainier, fifty miles from the city of Seattle; above all at Mount Hood, a short distance from the great city of Portland, the American national parks system and American forest service have developed entire areas for year round use, both as wonderful ski territory and for summer alpine visits; with good roads and low-cost hostel accommodation, which draws from the cities people who need this type of relaxation.
In British Columbia, the average person on the coast-and, after all, over two-thirds of the people of our province live on the coast- has no opportunity to visit our national parks. Yet some forty miles from Vancouver we have the fourth of these four great peaks in the Pacific northwest, in the Garibaldi area. Some years ago I had perhaps the happiest job I shall ever have in my life, that of surveying for the provincial government the principal winter sport areas throughout the west. In my survey which took me to Sun Valley, Mount Shasta, Mount Hood, Mount Baker and all through the Rocky mountains, I never saw any country to equal the Garibaldi country at the head of Howe sound.

So I suggest that if the national park system would start considering our national parks, not in terms of United States tourists but in terms of our own people, especially the sort of people who do not have an opportunity to travel very far from home in their two weeks' holidays, we would be in a far better position. I would rather see hundreds of low-cost hostels, such as the Americans have, throughout Banff and lake Louise than these glorified hotels which cost $15 to $20 a day. That is the type of thing which would make our parks truly national.
I should like to offer one other suggestion in connection with this national parks development, and it partly concerns this Ottawa development. We are having a tremendous development here; and I think Canadians even from as far away as British Columbia will admit that our national capital should be a beautiful place. More than that, however, the approaches to this country, our front doors, should also have a lovely appearance. In the city of Vancouver we are very fortunate in that some sixty years ago there were some citizens with singular foresight, who reserved that great peninsula, Stanley park, as a virgin stand of forest. I would say Stanley park is probably visited by more Canadians than any other park in this country; and of course it is as great a source of pride to our prairie Canadians as to the British Columbia Canadians.
On the north shore of the harbour entrance, however, is a long, low range of land at present covered with forest, which is a vacant Indian reserve. The people of Vancouver are most anxious to obtain that land and transform it into a park, so that for all time the spectacular sea approach to Vancouver city will remain a lovely thing. Unfortunately, however, the metropolitan parks board is having great difficulty in getting anywhere with the Indian affairs branch, which also comes under the Minister of Mines and Resources though in another category. Surely this is one matter about which not different departments of the government but this one department should do something, to see that, instead of being turned into gravel pits and an industrial development, the northern shore of the first narrows entrance to Vancouver is kept as green and lovely as is the Stanley park side, which is under the control of the city of Vancouver. The metropolitan parks board have done everything they can in the way of buying adjacent private land, and also in securing co-operation from the provincial government, but this is a problem solely for one -*epartment of the federal government, the

Department of Mines and Resources. It can bring together the unused Indian land which could be acquired by the metropolitan parks board and the national parks system, to ensure that for all time our loveliest harbour entrance shall remain as it is today.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask that you revert to government notices of motions in order that the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacKinnon) may move a motion for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.

subtopic: APPROVAL OP INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION SIGNED AT WASHINGTON ON DECEMBER 2, 1946
speechtext:
Government notices of motions.
Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (for the Secretary of State for External Affairs)' moved:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the international convention for the regulation of whaling, signed at Washington on December 2', 1946, and that this house do approve the same.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a short statement. This is a motion only, to approve Canada's participation with fourteen other countries in an international agreement for the regulation of the whaling industry. The senate has already discussed this matter and, after a brief debate, fully approved the international whaling convention signed by Canada at Washington on December 2, 1946. There is not a great deal I can usefully add to the discussion which occurred in the other place on February 12 of this year.
The Washington convention is not the first agreement in regard to whaling, in which Canada has taken part. Such a convention was signed at Geneva in 1931 and again at London in 1937. The present agreement is based on the principles of the London convention. One new feature of the Washington convention, however, is that under its provisions an international whaling commission is established for the first time, modeled on the Canada-United States international salmon and halibut commission. This commission will be composed of one representative from each participating country. Until the Washington convention comes into full effect, a protocol signed at Washington by the interested nations continues in force the regulations agreed upon in London.

Because of scientific and technical progress in the industry, it is necessary from time to time to revise and amend these international arrangements governing whaling activities. As in the case of the pacific fur seals, unless some international rules are observed, whales might also in time become almost extinct. There are many kinds of whales and this agreement seeks to eliminate over-fishing of any type. The killing of young whales is absolutely prohibited. Protection is also given to certain other varieties, and catches are limited in certain areas. Each of the contracting governments agrees to take proper measures to punish infractions of these regulations which come within their respective jurisdictions. The proposed international commission will have power to make regulations, but it will be the responsibility of the contracting governments to provide the necessary protection and to enforce such regulations.
Canada should take an active interest in the whaling industry because her Arctic territory is inhabited in considerable numbers by certain types of whales. The whale is particularly valuable in producing large quantities of oil and whalebone. Refined whale oil makes a valuable contribution to the world's supply of edible oils. In making its decisions, the new commission will take into consideration the interests of consumers of whale products. Also aborigines are free to kill whales for food under the Washington agreement.
Canadian commercial whaling activities have not been extensive. Since 1911 the industry has functioned to some extent on both the east and west coasts of Canada. In 1911 a whaling station was established by a private firm on the north shore of the St. Lawrence, but its operations ceased in 1915. A company operating on the Pacific coast commenced whaling operations in 1910. About 600 men were employed at one time by this firm, but its operations terminated in 1943. A new firm has recently been organized in British Columbia and is now applying for a licence to carry on whaling activities off the west coast. This company expects to use at least three whaling vessels this season. The adherence of Canada to the Washington convention will have no serious modifying effect on this particular project.
The nations which were represented at Washington and whose delegates signed the whaling convention were: Argentina, Australia, New Zealand, Brazil, Canada, Chile, Denmark, France, The Netherlands, Norway, Peru, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, the United Kingdom, the United States and the

Whaling Agreement
Union of South Africa. When six of the signing governments, including The Netherlands, Norway, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, the United Kingom and the United States, have deposited ratifications, this convention will come into force. It also becomes binding upon any other government which joins in ratification. Any contracting government may withdraw from the convention on June 30 of any year by giving six months' notice.
I believe it to be a wise thing for Canada to enter into this international agreement and to take its place in the world whaling industry.

Before the motion is carried, I wish to say a few words. I remember that I made a few jokes in 1935 when Mr. Bennett made this agreement a part of his social legislation. Social legislation was extended to whaling. It was quite funny, because whales were supposed to belong to the old order. He, however, brought whales into the new order; and they took up such a large space in it that everyone was astounded. I wonder what number of whales are caught in Canadian waters each year? Some people may learn something about whales through reading the agreement. The agreement is not with the resolution. I hope it will be in the schedule to the bill. We are told that it is about the same thing as the previous convention. Article 6 of the convention on the regulation of whaling, approval of which Mr. Bennett moved in the house on June 4, 1935, is found at page 3252 of Hansard of that date, and reads as follows: Article 6
The fullest possible use shall be made of the carcases of whales taken. In particular:
1. There shall be extracted by boiling or otherwise the oil from all blubber and from the head and the tongue and, in addition, from the tail as far forward as the outer opening of the lower intestine.
The provisions of this subparagraph shall apply only to such carcases or parts of carcases as are not intended to be used for human food.
We do not know what we are eating when we hear of these substitutes. Then there is article 10, which I can read in view of the fact 5849-241
that our lady colleague is not at present in the house. It reads as follows:
Article 10
1.	The high contracting parties shall obtain, with regard to the vessels flying their flags and engaged in the taking of whales, the most complete biological information practicable with regard to each whale taken, and in any case on the following points:
(a)	Date of taking;
(b)	Place of taking;
(e)	Species;
(d)	Sex;
(e)	Length: measured, when taken out of the water; estimated, if cut up in water:
(f)	When foetus is present, length and sex if ascertainable;
(g)	When practicable, information as to stomach contents.
2.	The length referred to in subparagraphs (e) and (f) of this article shall be the length of a straight line taken from the tip of the snout to the notch between the flukes of the tail.
That phraseology, Mr. Speaker, may be highly technical, but it is quite amusing to those who are profane.
Then there is article 17 which is full of solemnity. It shows how busy were the bureaucrats of the defunct league of nations. I presume that those of the united nations will have a similar occupation. Article 17 reads as follows:
Article 17
The present convention shall enter into force on the ninetieth day following the receipt by the secretary-general of the league of nations of ratifications or accessions on behalf of not less than eight members of the league or non-member states, including the Kingdom of Norway and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
As regards any member of the league or nonmember state on whose behalf an instrument of ratification or accession is subsequently deposited, the convention shall enter into force on the ninetieth day after the date of the deposit of such instrument.
And so it goes on. Is it necessary to have all that solemnity about whales? I can imagine all the fellows there in the big building of the league of nations at Geneva trying to find new words in order to show their importance in the drafting of a so-called convention like that. And by the way, it was not a convention; it was a draft convention that was left for anybody to accept or reject. But they called it a convention in order to make a greater impression on the people with regard to what they were doing in the whaling business. Now' the same thing is happening. We hoped that the united nations would be superior to the league of nations, but they indulge in the same trifling business as did the dead league. They will go on like that
Whaling Agreement

until we have a new war or until the people cease to be credulous enough to give them any importance.
We are all for the protection of the whaling industry. But why should people waste time in big efforts to write instruments like that one, which is the laughing stock of all those who peruse Hansard and see it. I was surprised, when I read it again, to see the false solemnity of those who want to impress us with words which may have a special meaning but are certainly not understood by those who harpoon whales.
When the matter comes before the committee I hope the minister will be kind enough to tell us what was the percentage of whales killed in Canadian waters during the last year. I hope he will tell us what was the total number of whales killed in Arctic and Antarctic waters, and what was the percentage killed in Canadian waters, so that we may know exactly what our interest is in the matter. I hope the minister will be kind enough to tell us that and also how many people in Canada are interested in the hunting or harpooning of whales. It is a fine sport. It cannot be indulged in, in a national park, but it deserves special consideration because one whale in itself is big business.

Mr. Speaker, there has not been a whale caught or killed in Canada since 1943, and I think that statement will provide answers to most of the questions asked by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank). The Washington convention made in 1946 provided for the convention being ratified by the various governments interested. Up to date the only governments which have ratified the convention are those of Iceland, the United Kingdom, the United States and Australia. The purpose of this resolution is to give ratification by the Canadian parliament to the agreement of 1946.
I was asked the powers that Canada could exercise in carrying out the regulations. Canada can police only her owm territorial waters and has the power to issue or cancel whaling licences. Japan is not a party to the whaling agreement, because that country is still under United States occupation. The whaling commission has not yet been formed, and it will come into existence when the convention comes into full force. Any country may reject the regulations on ninety days' notice according to article V, section 37, of the treaty.
In order to set the mind of the hon. member for Fraser Valley at rest in connection with oleomargarine, I may say that there is no thought of which I have any knowledge to use whale oil for the purpose of making oleomargarine. The hon. member for The Battle-fords (Mr. Campbell) asked about the division of whales among the member nations; but, as I said, no whales have been caught or killed in Canada for five years. What I am asking
for tonight is the ratification of the agreement entered into in 1946, which has been approved by the four or five countries I have indicated.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES-AIR SERVICE TO AUSTRALIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before Your Honour leaves the chair, there is a matter upon which I should like to say a few words and I think this can be done without keeping the house from getting into supply tonight. I am glad the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) is in his place, because what I wish to speak about relates to a matter under his supervision.
A few days ago on the orders of the day I directed certain questions to the minister with regard to air service between Canada and Australia. I asked the minister if he could indicate what progress was being made by Trans-Canada Air Lines in implementing the Canadian-Australian agreement, and I also asked this question:
Is it still government policy that when this service is put into effect by Canada it will be by the government-owned air line, and not by any private company?

Canadian-Australian Air Agreement
In reply to that question, the minister told me and the house that the T.C.A. had been fully occupied in establishing a transatlantic operation as well as an operation to South America, and therefore it had not been possible to give attention to the Australian service. I certainly have no quarrel with the minister's reply to that part of my question. In fact it is to the credit of the T.C.A. that it does not rush in, but it takes its time and makes sure that its operations are well established. However I was somewhat concerned over the nature of the minister's answer to my other question. Let me repeat the question that I asked in its precise terms, as recorded on page 3653 of Hansard for May 6, 1918. It was as follows:
Is it still government policy that when this service is put into effect by Canada it will be by the government-owned air line, and not by any private company?
The minister's reply to that question was as follows:
So far as government policy is concerned. I dare say when the matter is considered the government will be able to announce its policy.
I then asked:
Has there been any change?
But to that there was no reply. I may say that this is a matter which I have followed with some interest for a number of years. As the minister and other members of the government know, I have frequently expressed strong support of most aspects of the government's aviation policy.
On April 2. 1943, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made a basic statement with respect to the government's aviation policy as from that date. Part of that statement, as reported on page 1777 of Hansard of April 2, 1943, was in these words:
Trans-Canada Air Lines will continue to be the instrument of the government in maintaining all transcontinental air transport services and in operating services across international boundary lines and outside Canada.
Then, on page 1778 the Prime Minister gave these words as a conclusion to his statement of that day:
The policy of the Canadian government on air transport may be summed up as follows:
(a) The government sees no good reason for changing its policy that Trans-Canada Air Lines is the sole Canadian agency which may operate international air services.
And so on.
Next year, starting on March 17, 1944, we had an interesting and somewhat extended debate on civil aviation. This was begun by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply in a speech on that date, commencing at page

1571 of Hansard. On page 1579 of Hansard he quoted the statement of the Prime Minister which I have just quoted as having been made on April 2, 1943, and he confirmed that policy on behalf of the government, namely, that Trans-Canada Air Lines would be the sole Canadian agency to operate international air services.
The matter came up the next year in October, 1945, when the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act was amended. The amending bill provided for certain subsidiary corporations under T.C.A. for the handling of certain special operations. This subject was discussed in the course of that debate, and the minister reaffirmed the government's policy that international operations were to be carried on solely by Trans-Canada Air Lines.
The matter came up again the next year, 1946, in various ways, but I shall confine myself to the statement which the minister made in this house on August 30, 1946, as recorded at page 5640 of Hansard. On that date the minister announced to the house an agreement between Canada and Australia for air services between the two countries which had been signed at Ottawa on June 11. After making an oral statement to the house, the minister placed on the record a lengthy statement giving the details of the Canadian-Australian agreement, and part of that statement read as follows:
It-
Namely, the agreement that had been signed.
-provides for an exchange of traffic rights between Canada and Australia so that an air line designated by the government of Australia may put down and take up at Vancouver passengers. mail and cargo from Australia, while an air line designated by the government of Canada, which will be Trans-Canada Air Lines, may put down and take up in Australia traffic to and from Canada.
The significant phrase in that statement from which I have just quoted is the one to which I gave emphasis, namely, that the chosen instrument of Canada for the Canadian-Australian service would be Trans-Canada Air Lines.
We had a further discussion about aviation policy in the house last year, 1947, when the policy of the government was again reiterated. In other words, at no time since April 2, 1943, has there ever been any reluctance on the part of the government to state its international aviation policy. It has always been clear and definite that Trans-Canada Air Lines was to be the chosen instrument of the government for any service crossing an international border or for any service between

Canadian-Australian Air Agreement
Canada and any other country. The statement which the minister gave in reply to my question the other day was the first to show that there has been any reluctance to state the government's policy. Instead of answering my question in the manner in which I thought he would-I thought perchance he would tell me that I knew what government policy in this matter was, or words to that effect-he said:
So far as government policy is concerned I dare say when the matter is considered the government will be able to announce its policy.
I am not speaking with any heat about this matter, Mr. Speaker, and I am not anxious to throw out any unwarranted suspicions; in fact,
I want to cut my remarks short, so that the minister can reply tonight because I do not want this matter to be left over. My reason for raising it is that I feel it should be settled. Perchance last Thursday when I asked my question on the orders of the day the minister did not take time to realize its import; possibly he was just giving the stock answer for a minister to give, that the government s policy would be announced in due course. My hope is now that he will tell me that I am all wrong in my suspicions and in my lack of assurance about this matter. I hope he will tell me that it is still government policy that any air operation across the border or from Canada to any other country will, so far as Canada is concerned, be operated by Trans-Canada Air Lines.
Just one other thought I wish to express and it is this. We have in the service that goes from the Yukon across to Alaska a case where the policy of the government operating the service is implemented by T.C.A. subletting that particular operation to Canadian Pacific Air Lines. That may meet the letter of the law, but I am sure it does not meet the spirit of the government's policy. That would not be a proper implementation of the spirit of the Canadian-Australian agreement in which the government specifically said that Trans-Canada Air Lines would operate that service. There is more I could say, but I shall sit down for the specific purpose of enabling the minister to answer me and I hope he can set aside my fears and suspicions about this matter.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES-AIR SERVICE TO AUSTRALIA
speechtext:
I must say I do not understand the position of my hon. friend. He has spent five or ten minutes in approving the policy of the government, and then he asks me to deny it or confirm it. On the orders of the day a few days ago, he asked me the question he read out a few minutes ago, which was roughly to the effect, what was
T.C.A. doing in the Pacific and what was government policy in connection therewith? I answered that part of the question for which I am responsible. I am the minister responsible for Trans-Canada Air Lines and I told him exactly what Trans-Canada Air Lines was doing. I am not the minister who announces government policy on civil aviation. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) announced to the house two or three weeks ago that that responsibility had been transferred, and my hon. friend cheered when that announcement was made, so that he should know it better than any other man. Why he asked me the question I do not know. I do not think I am called upon to answer questions outside my jurisdiction.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES-AIR SERVICE TO AUSTRALIA
speechtext: What the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was asking was, will the minister confirm the policy that has been laid down by the government from time to time and by the minister himself?
